Sales Playbook
Riv Solar · Utility Service Program
The Pitch
Door approach for Energy Efficiency + Solar Program. State Contractor opening.
🚪 Door Opener
Hey, my name is [Name] — I'm a state contractor working on the current projects here in this area. I need to confirm with the homeowner that they're aware of the current projects being implemented in the neighborhood.
⚡ The Context Setup
Due to current events — specifically the national grid infrastructure crisis and recent outages — the state is requiring homes in this area to lower their current electric consumption. They've been implementing a program where a PPP fee covers the cost of these projects for qualifying homes. This covers infrastructure upgrades like replacing poles and restructuring underground wiring — and also covers energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy for the home.
Reference points to use: National grid emergency declaration, recent local outages (Long Beach), SCE PSPS wildfire shutoffs. See Resources tab for all links.
🔧 HVAC Lead-In
Part of what we're doing in this neighborhood is replacing HVAC units that have older refrigerant — specifically R-22 which is now federally banned — and providing home battery backup to support the grid during outages and shutoff events. We've already been servicing [nearby neighborhoods/cities] to get this done. Quick question — when was the last time you had your HVAC checked?
HVAC Response Flow
Branch based on what the homeowner says about their HVAC.
That's great — I'm glad you got that taken care of. The reason that matters is those older units run on R-22 refrigerant which is now banned. Since yours is newer, that's handled. What I do need to check is the battery backup side — because even with a newer HVAC, homes in this area are still being prioritized for the grid stabilization program. That's actually the bigger piece of what we're rolling out right now. [→ Transition to Solar + Battery program]
This is exactly why we're in the area. The program has limited funds — they can't cover every home — so it really comes down to the exact age and model of the unit. If they give the thumbs up, they cover the complete out-of-pocket expense to replace it. I can't guarantee it right now, but I can get your home assessed and get you in the queue. That's all we're doing today — just getting homes assessed. [→ Set the appointment]
This is exactly why we're here. Not sure if the program can cover it — it comes down to the budget they have allocated for this area and the age of the home. Quick question — what year was the house built? If they give the thumbs up, they cover the complete out-of-pocket expense to provide a unit for the home. [→ Set the appointment]
This is exactly why we're here. The program covers homes without traditional ducted HVAC — if the budget is available for this area and the home qualifies, they can cover the cost to provide you with a mini split system. It comes down to the area budget and the home. That's what the assessment determines. [→ Set the appointment]
Solar + Battery Pivot
How to transition from the HVAC conversation into the solar and battery program.
🔋 Pivot to Solar + Battery
The other component of what we're doing — and this ties directly to the grid issue — is home battery backup. The state is funding battery storage for qualifying homes because during PSPS events and infrastructure failures, homes with backup power take pressure off the grid. And since they're already running the installation, they include a solar system that lowers the home's rate on Edison — so instead of paying $0.44 per kilowatt, qualifying homes get locked in at a significantly lower rate for 25 years. No purchase. No loan. No lien on the home. The program owns the equipment — you just pay a lower utility rate.
Key framing: This is a utility service program — not solar sales. The battery is the grid stabilization component. The solar is how the rate gets lowered. Always lead with the grid story, not the solar pitch.
🏠 The Pullback
I'm not going to know right now if this home qualifies — that's what the assessment determines. What I can do is get you in the queue so when the team comes through this area, your home gets evaluated first. All I need from you today is to confirm you're the homeowner and set a time that works for you and anyone else in the household to sit down for about 20-30 minutes and go through the details.
Set the Appointment
The close of the door pitch. Get the appointment — not the sale.
📅 The Ask
I'm going to be honest with you — I don't make the decision on whether your home qualifies. That's determined during the assessment. My job is just to make sure qualifying homes in this area get evaluated before the funding window closes. When would work better for you — would [day] around [time] or [day] around [time] work better?
The goal at the door: Get the appointment. Not the close. Not the full pitch. Every word you say at the door beyond setting the appointment reduces your chances of getting it. Get in, confirm homeowner, set the time, leave.
✅ Confirmation Text (Send After)
Hey [Name], it's [Rep Name] — state contractor from earlier. Just confirming our appointment for [day] at [time]. I'll have your home's program assessment ready. See you then. [Name] · [Number] · License #132058
Solar Objections
Common objections and smokescreens. Tap to expand each one.
This is a trust objection, not a product objection. Don't defend solar — validate the concern and pivot to verification.
I completely understand that — honestly, there are a lot of companies in this space that have given people good reason to be skeptical. What I'd ask is one thing: look me up before you decide anything. My license is on the CSLB website — #132058 under Atreyu Thomas. Active, current, verified. This isn't a purchase. It's a utility service program — backed by CPUC regulations and state funding. You're not buying anything. You're switching who you buy power from, at a lower rate.
That's completely fair — and what I want to be clear about is this isn't solar in the way most people think about it. You're not buying panels, you're not taking on a loan, and there's no purchase. The program is a utility service — think of it like switching electricity providers. The solar panels and battery are owned by the company, not you. Your rate just goes from Edison's $0.44 per kilowatt down to a fraction of that. That's it. Would you be open to just seeing the numbers for your specific home?
This is not a no. This is a request for more time and inclusion. Honor it — and turn it into a scheduled sit with both present.
Absolutely — this is a household decision and I wouldn't want to move forward without both of you involved. When would work for you to have [spouse] here too? I'd rather sit down with both of you at the same time than have to explain it twice. Would [day] evening work, or is [day] better?
That's a fair concern. Here's the context: Edison's rates went up over 10% per year on average for the last 5 years. 2023 alone was a 19% increase. The 3.5% in the program is a cap — it's written into the agreement before you sign. Edison can raise their rate as much as the CPUC approves. Your program rate cannot exceed 3.5% in any given year. So the question isn't whether rates go up — they will. The question is whether you want your increase limited to 3.5% or unlimited.
No lien on your home — that's a very important distinction. This is a Power Purchase Agreement, not a loan. There is a UCC filing — but that's on the equipment itself, not your home. It simply establishes that the company owns their panels on your property. It does not affect your ability to sell, refinance, or transfer the home. California law also requires a simple notice to be recorded — it tells lenders that the company owns the panels. It is not an encumbrance on your title.
Make sure they're clear on the PPA vs lease distinction — the word "lease" appears on the CPUC disclosure checkbox but the agreement is titled Power Purchase Agreement on every page.
It's a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement — not a lease. The difference matters. A lease: you're renting equipment and owe payments regardless of output. A PPA: you're buying power at a fixed lower rate. You pay for what the system produces. If you sell the home, the agreement transfers to the new buyer — who takes over the lower utility rate, not a debt. Most buyers see that as a plus.
Good to know. Quick question — do you own the system or is it a lease/PPA? [If they own it:] Then you're paying full price for equipment that the program would have covered at no cost. The battery backup component may still be available for you depending on what you have. [If they have a lease/PPA:] Who's your provider? The rates and terms vary significantly. I can show you a direct comparison if you want to see where your current rate stands versus what the program offers.
The CPUC 3-bid rule applies to purchasing solar, not utility service programs. This is a critical distinction.
That's a good instinct — and it's accurate for solar purchases. The CPUC recommends multiple bids when you're buying a system. But this isn't a purchase. There's no cost, no loan, no equipment ownership. You're enrolling in a utility service program. You're not buying anything — so there's nothing to get multiple bids on. Think of it like switching from one utility provider to another. You wouldn't get multiple bids to switch from Edison to a lower-rate provider.
Honestly — you're not wrong to have that concern. There are bad actors in this space. Here's what I'd say: verify me before you believe anything I tell you. My license is on the California State License Board website — cslb.ca.gov — under #132058. Active and current. The program itself is referenced on your Edison bill — Apple Valley Choice Energy lists the Power Choice Program directly. The CPUC governs it. That's not something a scam company can fake. I'm not asking you to trust me. I'm asking you to verify it yourself.
Never leave without understanding what specifically they need to think about. "I'll think about it" with no follow-up is a slow no.
Of course — I want you to feel confident before any next step. Can I ask — what specifically would you like to think through? I'd rather answer any questions now so you have everything you need. [Listen to what they say — that's the real objection. Address that one thing.] If it's just time you need, no pressure — when would be a good time for me to follow up with you?
HVAC Objections
Common objections when pitching the HVAC energy efficiency program.
Glad to hear it. The program isn't just for units that are broken — it's about the refrigerant type and the efficiency rating. Older units running on R-22 are phased out by federal law, which affects your ability to service them going forward. Even if it's running, if it's an older unit, the question is whether it qualifies for the replacement program before the funding window closes. That's what the assessment determines.
This is actually your best angle — the whole point of the program is $0 cost.
That's the exact reason this program exists. There's no cost to you if the home qualifies — the state program covers the complete replacement expense. You don't pay anything out of pocket. The assessment just determines whether your home and unit qualify for the available funding. That's all we're doing today — seeing if you're eligible.
It's a state-funded energy efficiency program administered through licensed contractors — like the ESA program through SCE. The funding comes from state and federal energy efficiency mandates. I'm a licensed state contractor — you can verify that on the CSLB website. The program is also listed on SCE's website under the Energy Savings Assistance Program.
Understood — the program does require owner authorization for HVAC replacement since it's a structural improvement. If you can get your landlord on the phone or want to give me their contact info, I can reach out to them directly. This is actually a benefit to property owners — it's a fully covered upgrade to their unit.
Fair question. The program requires the home to qualify — not every home does. The unit has to meet the age and type criteria, and there's a limited budget allocated per area. If you qualify, the replacement is covered completely. There's no hidden cost. What you're committing to is the assessment — that's it. After the assessment, if your home qualifies, you decide whether to move forward.
Solar Sales Questions
Ask these in order. Listen more than you talk. The answers tell you exactly how to close.
The rule: Ask one question, then go quiet. Let them answer fully. The rep who listens more closes more. Every answer gives you the next angle.
1
Qualify ownership: "Are you the homeowner? And is it just you on the title, or is someone else on there too?"
2
Establish pain: "How much is your Edison bill running you right now? Has it gone up in the last year or two?"
3
Uncover awareness: "Have you heard anything about the programs Edison and the state are rolling out for grid stabilization and energy costs?"
4
Find the motivation: "If there was a way to cut your Edison bill roughly in half with no purchase and no upfront cost — is that something you'd at least want to understand?"
5
Surface the spouse: "Is [spouse/partner] usually involved in decisions like this? When would be a good time to have them part of the conversation?"
6
Handle hesitation: "What's the main thing that would make you hesitant about something like this?" — Then stop talking. Whatever they say is the real objection.
7
Tie down the logic: "If everything I've said checks out — your license, the CPUC documentation, the numbers for your specific home — what would stop you from moving forward?"
8
Set the ask low: "The only next step is an inspection to see if the home qualifies. No commitment, no cost. Can I get that on the calendar?"
HVAC Sales Questions
Qualifying questions for the HVAC energy efficiency program.
1
Qualify: "Are you the homeowner?" — If renting, pivot to landlord process.
2
Unit type: "What kind of HVAC do you have — central air, mini split, or window units?"
3
Age: "Do you know roughly how old the unit is? Or what year the house was built?"
4
Last service: "When was the last time someone came out and serviced or checked it?"
5
Pain: "Does it cool the house the way you want it to in the summer? Do you notice it running longer or not keeping up?"
6
Awareness: "Did you know R-22 refrigerant — which older units run on — is now federally banned? That means those units can't be serviced going forward."
7
The offer: "If the program covers the full replacement at no cost to you — is there a reason you wouldn't want that assessed?"
8
Set the appt: "I can get you in the queue for the assessment. What's the best time — would [day] or [day] work better?"
Golden Rules
Internalize these before sending a single message. Based on analysis of 38M+ messages.
📊 The Data
80%of sales need 5+ touches 45%SMS response rate 98%of texts are opened 44%of reps quit after 1 try
→
Never send more than 2 unanswered texts in a row. Call after the second.
→
Keep texts under 160 characters. Under 100 = 2–5x higher reply rates.
→
Always personalize — name, specific detail from the conversation, or their bill numbers.
→
Best text times: 10am–12pm. Best call times: weekdays 5–7pm, Sat 10am–1pm, Sun 11am–2pm.
→
Best call days: Tuesday and Wednesday. Avoid Monday mornings and Friday afternoons.
→
Space follow-ups 2–3 days apart. Daily = desperate. 5+ days = they forget you.
→
Multi-channel beats single channel by 28%. Text → Call → Email is the sequence.
→
Ghosting is almost never personal. It's overwhelm, a spouse, or timing.
→
When someone says "no thank you" — stop. No more texts. No more calls.
→
Every voicemail under 30 seconds. Long voicemails get deleted.
After Every Sit
Send within 2 hours. Every single time. This is the highest-ROI habit in the playbook.

The Break-Up Text
Use after 3+ unanswered touches. Creates a moment of decision. Consistently gets higher reply rates than standard follow-ups.
When to use: Only after 3+ attempts across multiple channels (not 3 texts in a row). Never after a hard no.
BREAK-UP Standard
Hey [Name], it's Atreyu. I don't want to keep reaching out if the timing isn't right. I'll leave the door open — you have my info whenever it makes sense. Take care.
BREAK-UP Softer Version
Hey [Name], still interested or good to close the file? No pressure either way — just want to respect your time.
Installed Accounts
Existing customers. Treat like family. Best source of referrals.
ANNUAL CHECK-IN
Hey [Name], it's Atreyu with your solar program. Reaching out to schedule your annual system check — want to confirm everything is running at full efficiency. Give me or Kishan a call when you get a chance. 213-660-6514 · License #132058
Referral opener: "If you have any neighbors or family dealing with high Edison bills, I'd love to help them the same way I helped you." Plant the seed. Don't push.
Cancelled Accounts
Already went through the process — that makes them warm. Don't assume — ask.
WIN-BACK General
Hey [Name], it's Atreyu. I know your project got cancelled a while back — just wanted to check in and see if anything has changed. No pressure, just want to make sure you have what you need if the timing is ever right.
WIN-BACK Roof Issue
Hey [Name], it's Atreyu. I know the roof was the holdup. Just checking in — if it would help, I can connect you with a roofer I trust in the area. Once that's handled the solar side is straightforward to pick back up.
Call Flow Guide
Not a script — a flow. Get them talking, then listen. The rep who listens more closes more.
1
Open warm: "Hey [Name], it's Atreyu — do you have a quick minute?" If busy: "When's a better time?" Lock in a specific time before hanging up.
2
Reference something specific: "I wanted to follow up from when we [met / talked about the program] — I know you were [thinking it over / talking to your spouse]."
3
Ask ONE question then go quiet: "Where are you at with everything?" — Then stop. Let them fill the silence. Whatever they say is the real objection.
4
Handle one objection at a time. Spouse → offer three-way call. Trust → CSLB verification. Escalator → Edison rate history. One thing at a time.
5
Tie down before hanging up: Never end with "I'll be in touch." Ask: "Would [day] at [time] work to sit down?" Get a commitment.
6
If not ready: "When would be a good time to check back in?" Lock in a date. Follow up exactly when you said you would.
Never on a call: Don't talk over objections. Don't list features when they didn't ask. Don't keep going after two clear no's. Don't ask more than one question at a time.

R-22 Refrigerant — Banned
R-22 refrigerant is federally phased out. Units running on R-22 cannot be serviced going forward. Use this to show homeowners directly.
Key talking point: R-22 was phased out on January 1, 2020 under the EPA Clean Air Act. No new R-22 can be manufactured or imported. Homeowners with R-22 units are sitting on equipment that can no longer be serviced after their current refrigerant runs out.
